Iron. A lustrous, ductile, and magnetic transition metal that is the most common element on Earth by mass. It makes up most of Earth's outer and inner core. It's the fourth most abundant element in the crust and humans have been smelting it for thousands of years, defining the historical shift from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age. Iron is chemically active and readily oxidizes in damp air to form rust. In living organisms, iron is critical: it forms the active core of hemoglobin and myoglobin, the proteins that transport oxygen through blood and muscle tissues.

In stars, iron marks a unique threshold. It's the heaviest element produced by ordinary stellar nucleosynthesis that doesn't require a supernova or neutron star merger, because fusing iron-56 actually absorbs energy rather than releasing it, triggering core collapse in massive stars. On Earth, iron forms the planet's core alongside nickel in a metallic alloy that generates our magnetic field through dynamo action in the liquid outer core. Iron exhibits ferromagnetism, the magnetic property so characteristic that it's named after the element itself. This magnetism vanishes when you heat iron above its Curie temperature at roughly one thousand forty-three Kelvin. Iron commonly shows oxidation states of plus two, the ferrous form, and plus three, the ferric form, though oxidation states from minus two to plus six are chemically possible. Major iron ores include hematite, which is ferric oxide; magnetite, ferric-ferrous oxide that acts as natural lodestone; and pyrite, iron disulfide, known colloquially as fool's gold. When alloyed with carbon, iron becomes steel, and small amounts of carbon atoms disrupt the crystal lattice to vastly increase strength, hardness, and durability. Iron binds oxygen in hemoglobin through an iron-containing porphyrin ring called heme, which gives red blood cells their colour and enables aerobic respiration. Iron also serves as the industrial catalyst in the Haber-Bosch process, the reaction that synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Carbon alloyed with iron produces steel, the backbone of modern structural engineering. Oxygen reacts with iron and water to form rust, and oxygen is also the terminal electron acceptor when iron-heme transports it. Nitrogen depends on iron catalysts in the Haber-Bosch process. Iron replaced copper alloys during the historical transition from the Bronze Age. Nickel forms iron-nickel alloys in planetary cores and iron meteorites. Potassium combines with iron to form ferrocyanide, which creates Prussian blue, a pigment used as an antidote for heavy metal poisoning.
